content: Swimmer's ear, medically referred to as otitis externa, is characterized by inflammation, irritation, or infection of the outer ear and ear canal. Symptoms of Swimmer's Ear: Discharge from the ear, which may appear yellow, yellow-green, pus-like, or have a foul odor. Ear pain that intensifies when the outer ear is pulled or manipulated. Hearing loss. Itching in the ear or ear canal. Causes of Swimmer's Ear: Swimming in polluted water can introduce water-loving bacteria, such as Pseudomonas, or, in rare cases, fungi, leading to infection. Other causes include: Inflammation and irritation of the bone and tissues at the base of the skull, known as malignant otitis externa. Scratching the ear or the inside of the ear canal. Foreign objects becoming lodged in the ear. Attempting to clean earwax with cotton swabs or small objects, which can irritate or damage the skin. Chronic swimmer's ear may result from: Allergic reactions to substances placed in the ear. Chronic skin conditions like eczema or psoriasis. High-Risk Groups: Swimmer's ear is relatively common, particularly among teenagers and young adults. It may occasionally be associated with middle ear infections (otitis media) or upper respiratory infections, such as colds. Diagnosis: A physical examination will be performed, including inspection of the ear. The ear and ear canal may appear red and swollen, with scaly or shedding skin inside the canal. Pain may increase when the outer ear is touched or moved. Swelling in the outer ear may obscure the eardrum, or the eardrum may have a perforation (a hole). A sample of ear fluid may be collected and sent to a laboratory to identify any bacteria or fungi. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: If you develop symptoms of swimmer's ear. If you notice any ear discharge. If symptoms worsen or persist despite treatment. If new symptoms arise, such as fever or pain and redness behind the ear on the skull. Treatment Options: Antibiotic ear drops are typically prescribed for 10 to 14 days. If the ear canal is significantly swollen, a wick may be placed in the ear to help the drops reach the end of the canal. Your healthcare provider can demonstrate how to use this. Additional treatments may include: Oral antibiotics if there is a middle ear infection or if the infection has spread beyond the ear. Corticosteroids to reduce itching and inflammation. Pain relievers, such as acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin). Acetic acid (vinegar) ear drops. For chronic swimmer's ear, long-term or repeated treatments may be necessary to prevent complications. Applying something warm to the ear may help alleviate pain. Prognosis: With proper treatment, swimmer's ear typically resolves without complications. Possible Complications: The infection may spread to surrounding areas, including the skull bone. In elderly individuals or those with diabetes, a severe infection called malignant otitis externa may occur. This condition requires treatment with high-dose intravenous antibiotics. Prevention: Protect the ears from further damage: Avoid scratching the ears or inserting cotton swabs or other objects into them. Keep the ears clean and dry, and prevent water from entering the ears during activities like showering, shampooing, or bathing. Thoroughly dry the ears after exposure to moisture. Avoid swimming in polluted water. Use earplugs while swimming. Consider using a mixture of one drop of alcohol and one drop of white vinegar in the ears after they get wet. The alcohol and acid in the vinegar help inhibit bacterial growth.
